title: Owning Your Own: sin, si, sitt, sine
goal: Choose the correct possessive when the subject owns the noun.

objectives.statement: Choose the correct possessive when the subject owns the noun.

sections.title: A busy morning at the cabin

spans.value: Lina, Oskar, Jonas, Nora, and Emil are leaving a cabin after a weekend away. Everyone is packing, but several belongings are still scattered around.
De ligger ved siden av sekken din.
Bra. Jonas leter også etter nøklene sine.

blocks.translation: Good. Jonas is also looking for his own keys.

spans.value: Han pakker bilen sin nå. Han har lagt jakka si i baksetet, men mobilen hans ligger fortsatt på bordet.

blocks.translation: He’s packing his own car now. He has put his own jacket on the back seat, but his phone is still on the table.

spans.value: Da må han hente mobilen sin før han drar.

blocks.translation: Then he has to get his own phone before he leaves.

spans.value: Ja. Nora og Emil rydder rommet sitt og samler koppene sine.

blocks.translation: Yes. Nora and Emil are tidying their own room and collecting their own cups.

spans.value: The situation is simple: each person needs to find and pack the things that belong to them. Norwegian marks this relationship more clearly than English does.
Look at what belongs to Jonas:

en.value: Jonas is looking for his own keys.
He is packing his own car.

no.value: Han har lagt jakka si i baksetet.

en.value: He has put his own jacket on the back seat.

spans.value: In each sentence, the subject and the owner are the same person. Jonas is looking for Jonas’s keys, packing Jonas’s car, and moving Jonas’s jacket. Norwegian uses a

sections.title: When the subject owns the noun

spans.value: when a third-person subject owns the noun in the same clause.

en.value: Jonas is washing his own car.
Nora is packing her own bag.
Emil is selling his own house.
They find their own tickets.

spans.value: The subject is Jonas. The car belongs to Jonas, so Norwegian uses
The subject is Nora. The bag belongs to Nora, so Norwegian uses
The subject is Emil. The house belongs to Emil, so Norwegian uses
The subject is de. The tickets belong to them, so Norwegian uses
This pattern works with the third-person subjects
, as well as with names and noun phrases.

no.value: Han tar på seg jakka si.

en.value: He puts on his own jacket.
She opens her own letter.
The cat eats its own food.
The students submit their own assignments.

spans.value: Does the possessed noun belong to the subject of this clause?

items.value: If no, use an ordinary third-person possessive such as

sections.title: The ending follows the possessed noun

spans.value: The form does not tell you whether the owner is male, female, or plural. It agrees with the noun that is owned.
Compare four things belonging to the same person:

en.value: Jonas finds his own backpack.
Jonas finds his own book.
Jonas finds his own passport.
Jonas finds his own glasses.

spans.value: Jonas remains the owner in every sentence, but the form changes because the possessed noun changes.
In Bokmål, many feminine nouns can also be treated as masculine. You may therefore encounter both
, depending on the noun forms the speaker uses. Keep the noun form and possessive form consistent.

no.value: Hun legger boka si på bordet.

en.value: She puts her own book on the table.

no.value: Hun legger boken sin på bordet.

en.value: She puts her own book on the table.

sections.title: Sin is not simply another word for his

spans.value: without clearly showing whether the owner is the subject. Norwegian makes an important contrast.

en.value: Jonas is washing his own car.
Jonas is washing his car—the car of another male person.

spans.value: In the first sentence, the car belongs to Jonas, the subject. In the second, it belongs to another man or boy already known from the context.
The same contrast appears with a female subject:

en.value: Nora is packing her own bag.
Nora is packing her bag—the bag of another female person.

no.value: Nora og Emil rydder rommet sitt.

en.value: Nora and Emil are tidying their own room.

no.value: Nora og Emil rydder rommet deres.

en.value: Nora and Emil are tidying their room—the room belonging to other people.

spans.value: The English translations can sound similar, so it helps to add
Consider Jonas and Oskar at the cabin.

no.value: Jonas legger mobilen sin i sekken.

en.value: Jonas puts his own phone in the backpack.

spans.value: The subject is Jonas, and the phone belongs to Jonas.

no.value: Oskar legger mobilen hans i sekken.

en.value: Oskar puts his phone in the backpack.

spans.value: can refer to Jonas. The subject is Oskar, but the phone belongs to someone else.
Now make Jonas the subject again:

no.value: Jonas tar mobilen sin ut av sekken.

en.value: Jonas takes his own phone out of the backpack.

spans.value: The physical phone may be the same in all three sentences. The possessive changes because the clause subject changes.

sections.title: A common mistake: matching the owner

spans.value: A frequent mistake is to choose
for several owners. That is not how these forms work.

First decide whether the subject owns the noun.
Then match the possessive to the possessed noun.

no.value: Jonas tar på seg jakka si.

en.value: Jonas puts on his own jacket.

no.value: Nora tar på seg jakka si.

en.value: Nora puts on her own jacket.

spans.value: is feminine. The owner’s gender makes no difference.
Now compare one person and several people:

en.value: Nora finds her own passport.

no.value: Nora og Emil finner passet sitt.

en.value: Nora and Emil find their own passport.

spans.value: is neuter singular. A plural subject does not automatically require
only when the possessed noun is plural:

en.value: Nora finds her own tickets.

no.value: Nora og Emil finner billettene sine.

en.value: Nora and Emil find their own tickets.

spans.value: In the examples in this chapter, the possessive follows the noun. The noun then normally has its definite form.

en.value: his or her own car
his or her own jacket
his, her, or their own house
his, her, or their own keys

spans.value: Use the whole phrase as a unit when speaking and writing.

en.value: She locks her own door.
He tidies his own room.
They bring their own suitcases.

spans.value: Do not leave the noun indefinite in this pattern.

en.value: She finds her own bag.

spans.value: The important target remains the possessive choice, but producing the familiar definite-noun pattern helps the result sound natural.
Jonas comes back into the room. Lina has found his keys, and Oskar points to the phone on the table.
Jonas, jeg fant nøklene dine under sofaen.

blocks.translation: Jonas, I found your keys under the sofa.

spans.value: Takk! Jeg leter alltid etter tingene mine.

blocks.translation: Thanks! I’m always looking for my things.

spans.value: Lina now gives Jonas the keys.

en.value: Lina gives Jonas his keys.

spans.value: ? Lina is the subject, but Jonas owns the keys. The subject and owner are different.

no.value: Jonas legger nøklene sine i lomma.

en.value: Jonas puts his own keys in his pocket.

spans.value: ? Jonas is now the subject and the owner of the keys.

en.value: Oskar gives him his phone.
Jonas checks his own phone.

spans.value: These pairs show why you must identify the subject in each clause. Ownership has not changed, but the grammatical subject has.

sections.title: Transfer to a new situation: closing the office

spans.value: The setting now changes. Three colleagues are leaving an office at the end of the day. They need to put away their own equipment and avoid taking someone else’s belongings.

en.value: Amina turns off her own computer.
Petter closes his own window.
They collect their own papers.

spans.value: But Petter also notices Amina’s bag:

no.value: Petter setter veska hennes ved døra.

en.value: Petter puts her bag by the door.
Amina takes her own bag.

items.value: Does the noun belong to the subject?
If it does, which form matches the possessed noun?

prompt.value: Read the cabin sentence and choose the complete interpretation that identifies the subject, the possessed item, and whether the item belongs to the subject. Do not score agreement yet.

options.text: Subjektet er Jonas, tingen er jakka, og Jonas eier den selv — The subject is Jonas, the item is the jacket, and Jonas owns it himself.
options.why: The subject Jonas owns the jacket, so the sentence expresses his own jacket.

options.text: Subjektet er Jonas, tingen er jakka, og Nora eier den — The subject is Jonas, the item is the jacket, and Nora owns it.
options.why: The sentence does not make Nora the owner.

options.text: Subjektet er Nora, tingen er jakka, og Nora eier den selv — The subject is Nora, the item is the jacket, and Nora owns it herself.
options.why: The subject in the sentence is Jonas, not Nora.

options.text: Subjektet er Jonas, tingen er passet, og Jonas eier den selv — The subject is Jonas, the item is the passport, and Jonas owns it himself.
options.why: The possessed item in the sentence is the jacket, not the passport.

prompt.value: Every item belongs to the sentence subject. Fill each blank with the correct member of sin–si–sitt–sine. Choose from the possessed noun gender and number; the owner gender is irrelevant.
Complete each cabin sentence. Use a reflexive form when the subject owns the item; use hans, hennes, or deres when a named other person owns it. Agreement is secondary in this activity.

explanation.value: Sin/si/sitt/sine refers back to the clause subject and agrees with the possessed noun; hans/hennes/deres identifies another owner.

Write five short Norwegian sentences about colleagues closing an office and collecting personal belongings. Use original office wording.
